analysis.one_liner: Eliminates copays and deductibles for insulin and related supplies under Medicare and Medicaid.
analysis.headline: The Insulin Access for All Act, with 51 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to House committees in June 2021 and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend Medicare and Medicaid so that people enrolled in those programs pay nothing out of pocket — no deductible, copay, or coinsurance — for insulin and the supplies used to inject it. It would have taken effect January 1, 2022. The bill never moved past its committee referrals.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare Part D enrollees and Medicaid beneficiaries who use insulin. Roughly a million-plus Medicare beneficiaries and many Medicaid recipients have diabetes; today they can face copays or deductibles for a drug they cannot skip. The bill removes that out-of-pocket cost entirely for insulin and injection supplies.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare and Medicaid patients who use insulin

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any deductible, copayment, coinsurance, or other cost sharing for insulin and associated injection supplies under the Medicare Part D drug benefit.
Adds insulin and injection supplies to the list of items exempt from Medicaid cost sharing, including under the alternative cost-sharing rules for higher-income beneficiaries.
Sets the effective date at January 1, 2022, with a transition window for states whose Medicaid plans need state legislation to comply.

analysis.who_pays: The Medicare program, Part D plans, and Medicaid (split between federal and state budgets) absorb the cost of the eliminated copays. The bill does not lower insulin list prices, so drug makers keep charging what they charge — it is simply paid by the programs rather than the patient, and Part D premiums could edge up as plans absorb the difference.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare, Medicaid budgets, and Part D plans

drawbacks.text: The bill addresses only out-of-pocket costs, not the underlying price of insulin; manufacturers would keep selling at current list prices, now billed to Medicare and Medicaid instead of patients.
Eliminated cost sharing shifts spending onto federal and state budgets and Part D plans, which can recoup it through higher premiums paid by all enrollees.
It does nothing for people with employer insurance, marketplace plans, or no insurance at all, who face some of the steepest insulin costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For insulin-dependent Medicare and Medicaid patients, eliminating cost sharing is a direct, meaningful gain — skipped doses to save money are a documented, dangerous practice. The main honest objection is design: the bill removes the patient's cost without touching the price, so the programs and other premium-payers absorb high manufacturer prices rather than pressuring them down. It is a targeted access fix, not a price fix.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees and a Health subcommittee in June 2021, and no committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Rush introduced the bill on June 24, 2021, with 38 original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, and days later to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health.
Cosponsorship grew to 51 members, all Democrats; no Republican cosponsored it.
No markup, hearing vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insulin manufacturers keep selling at existing list prices, and Medicare and Medicaid patients continue paying whatever copays their plans impose. The members and committees that left the bill untouched face no cost for inaction.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insulin makers and the status quo

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, growing the roster from 38 original cosponsors to 51; no Republican joined.

sides.party_line_note: All 51 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the record shows no floor vote where a partisan split could be measured.

industries.note: The bill removes the patient cost barrier without touching list prices, so manufacturers would keep selling insulin at current prices, now paid by Medicare and Medicaid instead of patients. Zero copays likely sustain or raise their sales volume.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D plans and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Plans would have to absorb the eliminated copays and coinsurance for insulin, or shift the cost into premiums paid by all enrollees. Their interest in preserving cost sharing runs against patients' need for affordable insulin.
States would pick up part of the eliminated cost sharing for Medicaid beneficiaries, a real budget cost, in exchange for beneficiaries getting insulin without out-of-pocket charges.
